title: Converting CNF to DNF
formal:
Determine the worst-case minimum DNF term count of a Boolean function representable by a \(k\)-CNF on \(n\) variables. More precisely, for integers \(1\le k\le n\), let \(\mathcal C_{n,k}\) be the set of Boolean functions on \(\{0,1\}^n\) representable as a conjunction of clauses, each containing at most \(k\) literals. Define
\[
d(f)=\min\{\text{number of terms in }D:D\text{ is a DNF on the same variables and }D(x)=f(x)\text{ for every }x\in\{0,1\}^n\},
\]
\[
M(n,k)=\max_{f\in\mathcal C_{n,k}}d(f).
\]
Supply a mathematical description of a real-valued function \(g\) on \(\mathcal D=\{(n,k)\in\mathbb Z^2:1\le k\le n\}\), with a complete Lean proof that
\[
\forall(n,k)\in\mathcal D,\qquad
|g(n,k)-M(n,k)|\le\frac1{100}.
\]
The error is measured in the unnormalized number of DNF terms. The approximation need not be integer-valued. This finite-parameter determination is an editorial extension of the source’s request to close the gap between exponential upper and lower bounds.
why: The same Boolean function can have very different sizes in conjunctive and disjunctive normal form. This question measures the largest unavoidable number of DNF terms when only the input clause width and number of variables are fixed, separating an inherent representation cost from the performance of any particular conversion algorithm.
status_note: The checked 2013 primary source leaves the general minimum-DNF-term exponential gap open. The 2022 primary paper improves a monotone special case and counts general prime implicants, while the June 2026 formalization concerns classical exponential-blowup examples. The individual review and bounded later-work check on 16 September 2026 found no determination of the full general extremal term-count function. This card explicitly extends the source’s asymptotic question to pointwise approximation of M(n,k) within 1/100; that acceptance target is not itself a historically sourced conjecture. The review is not an exhaustive current-openness certificate.

progress.text: The December BRICS report gives a bounded-width DNF upper bound in Lemma 4 and defines size as the number of terms. Its printed lemma assumes \(1\le k\le n/100\); the seminar later summarizes the bound without that displayed regime.
On converting CNF to DNF appears in Theoretical Computer Science 347(1–2), pages 325–335; the 2013 question cites this journal version.
Schneider poses the problem of closing the gap between the upper bound and the block-parity lower bound in Seminar 13331, Section 6.19.
SAT 2022, Corollary 34, proves \(d(f)\le n\,2^{n(1-0.282/k)}\) for monotone \(k\)-CNFs; the general signed-clause extremal function is not determined.
An Archive of Formal Proofs entry formalizes classical exponential blowup examples in Isabelle; it does not supply matching full-domain extremal bounds for the present quantity.

sentences: For each variable count n and clause width k, the target is the largest minimum number of DNF terms needed to represent an n-variable k-CNF function.
The DNF must agree on every assignment using the same variables, while its terms may overlap and may have arbitrary width.
The source leaves a gap between exponential upper and lower bounds, and later improvements for monotone formulas do not determine the general case.
The card explicitly extends that asymptotic question to a real-valued description of the extremal function within one hundredth of a term at every admissible pair.
A complete Lean proof must certify the universal upper and extremal lower bounds, thereby identifying the inherent representation cost rather than a conversion algorithm’s running time.

definitions:
The variables are \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), with values in \(\{0,1\}\). A literal is \(x_i\) or \(\neg x_i\); at an assignment \(a\), these have values \(a_i\) and \(1-a_i\), respectively. A clause is a disjunction of literals and a term is a conjunction of literals. A CNF is a finite conjunction of clauses; a DNF is a finite disjunction of terms. Width at most \(k\) bounds the number of literals in each CNF clause, not the number of clauses. Both positive and negative literals are permitted, and no monotonicity, occurrence bound or bound on the number of clauses is assumed.

For a concrete finite representation, identify literals with signed indices \((i,b)\), where \(1\le i\le n\), \(b=1\) denotes \(x_i\), and \(b=0\) denotes \(\neg x_i\). A clause is a set of at most \(k\) such signed indices with at most one sign per variable, and a CNF is a set of these clauses. Repeated literals and clauses have no effect; clauses containing both signs of a variable are tautological and may be omitted. A term is likewise a set of signed indices with at most one sign per variable, with no width bound other than \(n\), and a DNF is a set of terms. A contradictory term may be omitted. These normalizations do not change the represented functions or their minimum DNF term counts.

An empty conjunction has value one and an empty disjunction has value zero. Thus an empty CNF represents one, an empty clause makes a CNF zero, an empty DNF represents zero, and the singleton DNF consisting of the empty term represents one. In particular, \(d(0)=0\) and \(d(1)=1\). The ambient variable set has size \(n\), but a represented function need not depend on every variable. Equivalence means equality of Boolean values on all \(2^n\) assignments. No auxiliary variables, projection, merely equisatisfiable encoding or approximation of the Boolean function is allowed. Distinct DNF terms may be satisfied simultaneously.

The size being minimized is the number of terms, irrespective of their lengths. It is not the number of literal occurrences, the serialized bit length, the number of satisfying assignments, or the number of all inclusion-minimal implicants. There are finitely many functions and normalized formulas at each \((n,k)\), and every function has a DNF, so the stated minima and maximum exist. This is a structural extremal question. It imposes no computational model, running-time or space bound for converting an individual formula or evaluating the supplied mathematical answer; the signed-index representation fixes the objects being counted rather than an algorithmic resource promise.
answer_criterion:
Supply \(g\), a formula, certified evaluation rule or other unambiguous mathematical description of its values in terms of \(n,k\), and a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of the displayed pointwise error bound throughout \(\mathcal D\). The proof must establish both the universal upper bound for every permitted \(k\)-CNF function and the corresponding extremal lower bound at every admissible parameter pair. Equivalently, certified real bounds \(L(n,k)\le M(n,k)\le U(n,k)\) of width at most \(1/50\) qualify through their midpoint. Exact determination is welcome but is not required, and the answer need not be integer-valued.

Merely renaming the defining maximum and minimum, or giving exhaustive enumeration of all CNF and DNF representations as the answer, does not determine the requested extremal law. Finite tables, one-sided estimates, bounds only for monotone formulas, or asymptotic estimates with unspecified constants do not meet the full-domain tolerance. This numerical acceptance precision belongs to the editorial extension and is not attributed to the 2013 source.

context_blocks.text: Schneider’s 2013 question asks how large the smallest equivalent DNF of a \(k\)-CNF can be and explicitly measures size by the number of terms. It asks to close an exponential upper/lower gap; it does not pose an output-sensitive algorithmic problem or state that a particular lower-bound example is always extremal.

The source reports the upper bound \(2^{n(1-1/(100k))}\) and the block-parity lower bound \(2^{n(1-1/k)}\) when \(k\) divides \(n\). Block parity here is the conjunction of prescribed parity conditions on disjoint blocks of \(k\) variables. These estimates agree in the order of the exponent saving while leaving its precise value undetermined.

The current card makes the underlying extremal function \(M(n,k)\) explicit and asks for a pointwise determination within \(1/100\) term on all \(1\le k\le n\). This is the authorized quantitative extension used by the catalogue, stronger than closing only the source’s asymptotic gap. The source is retained as provenance for the quantity, not presented as having demanded this finite-parameter precision.

Miltersen, Radhakrishnan and Wegener’s December 2003 report defines DNF size by the number of terms and proves the bounded-width upper estimate in Lemma 4. Their main parameterized result instead constrains the number of CNF clauses; that parameter is distinct from the clause-width parameter \(k\) used here.

Mossé, Sha and Tan obtain the bound \(n\,2^{n(1-0.282/k)}\) for monotone \(k\)-CNFs with \(k\ge2\), where monotone means that no variable is negated. Their more general results count all prime implicants: terms implying the function from which no literal can be removed while retaining that implication. In general these terms need not all be present in a smallest equivalent DNF, so that counting problem is distinct from \(M(n,k)\).

A June 2026 Isabelle formalization proves exponential size blowup for specific CNF and DNF families. Its lower-bound examples and formula-size measure do not determine the full extremal term-count function asked for here.

Applied the explicitly authorized quantitative extension to the underlying function M(n,k), with a real-valued answer and absolute 1/100 tolerance, and disclosed that this is stronger than the source’s asymptotic gap-closing request. Do not identify the displayed block-parity lower bound with a universally tight upper bound. checked_sources: Read the complete canonical TCS-0799 record, including legacy and saved primary locator, and the applicable RULES quantitative-target and Lean-acceptance instructions. Downloaded the standalone Dagstuhl Seminar 13331 report and read the actual Section 6.19 on printed page 70, standalone PDF page 31. The saved full-issue pointer is PDF page 72. The source asks for minimum equivalent DNF term count, reports 2^{n(1-1/(100k))} versus block-parity 2^{n(1-1/k)} when k divides n, and asks to close the gap. It does not specify an algorithmic running-time model or assert equality with the lower example. Suggested proof approaches in the source were omitted from card content.

Read the March 27, 2003 ECCC TR03-017 preprint for the definitions and its polynomial-clause-count main theorem, then separately obtained and read the December 2003 BRICS RS-03-45 report. The latter contains the relevant bounded-width Lemma 4 on printed page 7/PDF page 9: width r<=n/100 implies dnfsize(f)<=2^{n-n/(100r)}. Read its proof and distinguished its scope from the paper’s main bound in terms of the number of clauses m. The March and December versions have different statements and numbering. Confirmed the December report publication date from the BRICS repository and the 2005 journal metadata and abstract from the publisher; did not claim to have read the final journal PDF.

Read the actual SAT 2022 PDF by Mossé, Sha and Tan: definitions of implicants and completions, the distinction between the Blake Canonical Form and a minimum equivalent DNF, Theorem 14 on general prime-implicant counts, and Section 5.2 including Theorem 32, Fact 33, Corollary 34 and Theorem 35. The improved n*2^{n(1-0.282/k)} minimum-term bound is specifically for monotone k-CNFs. The universal signed-clause question is not settled by the base-3 count of all prime implicants.

Read the June 15, 2026 Archive of Formal Proofs entry and downloaded its actual proof outline, internally dated June 16. Read the formula-size definition and the exp-blowup-from-CNF-to-DNF and exp-blowup-from-DNF-to-CNF theorem statements on outline page 11. These assert existence of linear-size formulas forcing exponential equivalent formula size; they neither optimize the DNF term count over all width-k inputs nor determine M(n,k). No independent Isabelle proof replay was performed.

Performed bounded later-source searches through September 16, 2026 for bounded-width CNF-to-DNF conversion, minimum DNF size, block parity, extremal k-CNF formulas and subsequent references to the 2005 and 2022 papers. Read primary abstracts for arXiv:2412.20493v1 (December 29, 2024), which concerns fixed-Hamming-weight satisfying assignments of k-CNFs capturing thresholds, and arXiv:2506.07268v1 (June 8, 2025), which constructs formulas with a prescribed number of models. They concern distinct quantities. Results on k-DNF resolution, approximate polynomial degree, backdoor DNFs and practical model enumeration were not conflated with the present unrestricted extremal term-count target. No matching full resolution was found; this does not certify exhaustive current openness.

The target M(n,k) with full-domain absolute 1/100 accuracy is an authorized editorial extension, not a verbatim historical conjecture. The audit specifically rejected replacing the source with the unsupported universal equality M(n,k)=2^{n(1-1/k)}: for example, the conjunction of two independent positive triangle 2-CNFs on six variables needs nine DNF terms, whereas that expression equals eight. This scope check was not turned into a public solution hint or an archive claim about the actual source problem.
